overview:
Along the Indus and the now largely dry Ghaggar-Hakra river system, across what is today Pakistan, northwestern India and part of Afghanistan, farming villages descended from Neolithic settlements like Mehrgarh grew into something without precedent in South Asia. By around 2600 BCE — the start of what archaeologists call the Mature Harappan phase — cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Ganweriwala and Rakhigarhi anchored a network of more than a thousand known settlements spread over roughly a million square kilometres, making it the most extensive of the Bronze Age's early civilisations in sheer area. What survives is above all a landscape of engineering: streets laid on rough grids, houses of standardised kiln-fired brick, wells and bathing platforms in ordinary homes, and covered street drains that amount to the earliest urban sanitation known anywhere. Weights cut to a shared binary standard turn up from Gujarat to the Afghan foothills, as do the same bead types, the same pottery shapes, the same square steatite seals carved with animals and a short line of signs.

Those seals travelled. Harappan and Harappan-style objects appear at Ur, Kish and other Mesopotamian sites, and in the Gulf and Oman, and Sumerian texts speak of a distant trading partner called Meluhha that most scholars — though not all, and not conclusively — identify with the Indus world. Carnelian, lapis, copper, timber and cotton moved along these routes. But the Indus cities look strikingly unlike their trading partners in one respect: no palace has been identified, no temple, no royal tomb, no convincing depiction of a king or an army. Housing quality varies less than at Ur or Memphis. Whether this reflects a genuinely different kind of authority — a merchant oligarchy, a ritual order, competing city-states — or simply our failure to recognise the evidence is unresolved, and the argument runs hot because the Indus script, some 4,000 short inscriptions averaging five signs, has never been deciphered and may never be. There is no bilingual text, no long document, and no agreement on what language lies underneath, though a Dravidian or Elamo-Dravidian connection is the most commonly argued case.

After about 1900 BCE the cities emptied. Settled area shrank, the large centres were abandoned or thinned out, and population shifted eastward toward the Ganges plain. The nineteenth-century idea of a violent Aryan conquest has been largely abandoned; the current weight of evidence points to a slow environmental squeeze, as a weakening summer monsoon dried the monsoon-fed rivers and made the flood-recession agriculture that fed the cities unreliable, pushing communities toward smaller settlements and hardier crops. Ancient DNA from a Mature Harappan burial at Rakhigarhi, published in 2019, showed a mix of Iranian-related farmer and indigenous South Asian ancestry with no steppe pastoralist component, suggesting the steppe-derived ancestry now widespread in South Asia arrived after the cities had already declined. Late Harappan material culture persisted for centuries; the civilisation did not so much end as disperse.
significance: This was one of the handful of places on earth where cities, writing, standardised measurement and long-distance trade emerged independently, and it did so at a scale that dwarfed contemporary Egypt and Mesopotamia in territory while leaving almost none of the monumental self-advertisement those societies produced. That absence is itself the point: the Indus case is the strongest evidence available that complex urban society did not require kings, conquest and temple hierarchies, and it forces archaeologists everywhere to ask whether they have been reading power into the wrong kinds of ruins. Its rediscovery in the 1920s also rewrote South Asian history, pushing the region's urban past back two millennia — with consequences that remain politically live in India and Pakistan today, where questions about the script, the language and the relationship between the Harappans and later Vedic culture carry weight far beyond the excavation trench. And its unravelling under a drying climate has become one of the most cited cases in the study of how environmental stress dismantles cities.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews plus the published Rakhigarhi genome study and the PNAS work on Harappan river landscapes; the dataset itself holds no events beneath this story, so the map can show nothing of its internal sequence — no founding of Mohenjo-daro, no abandonment horizon, no trade contact. The deeper gap is in the record itself: with an undeciphered script and no readable texts, essentially everything about Harappan politics, religion, law and language is inference from material remains, the dates are archaeological approximations rather than fixed years, and major sites including Ganweriwala remain largely unexcavated.
